name: Obetrol (amphetamine salts)

lead: Obetrol was a US prescription diet pill from the 1950s and 1960s combining amphetamine and methamphetamine salts, marketed for obesity. It suppressed appetite to produce weight loss.

It acted through the central nervous system effects typical of amphetamines. The FDA approved it in 1960 and withdrew approval in 1973. A later methamphetamine-free reformulation became Adderall, approved for ADHD in 1996.

paras: It was prescribed as a tablet for exogenous obesity. No drug marketed as Obetrol exists today; it is cited as a historical diet pill.
Amphetamines carry misuse and cardiovascular concerns. The 1973 withdrawal cited weak supporting research as well as the speed-epidemic context. It is no longer sold.

angle.text: Obetrol was an amphetamine-based diet pill that suppressed appetite, so people ate less and lost weight. It is of historical interest as the ancestor of Adderall.

lead: Obetrol was a prescription diet pill sold in the United States from 1960 until its approval was withdrawn in 1973. It combined four amphetamine and methamphetamine salts, and it was used to help people lose weight by reducing appetite alongside a lower-calorie diet, the same fat-loss goal that drives cutting in looksmaxxing today.[1][2]

The original 10 mg tablet reportedly held 2.5 mg each of methamphetamine saccharate, methamphetamine hydrochloride, racemic amphetamine sulfate and dextroamphetamine sulfate, with a 20 mg version doubling the amounts.[1] The FDA approved the formula in January 1960 and withdrew approval in September 1973, citing weak supporting research.[1]

Rexar later dropped the methamphetamine salts, and after Richwood Pharmaceuticals acquired Rexar in 1993 the reformulated product was renamed Adderall, which was approved for ADHD in February 1996.[1] No drug marketed as Obetrol exists today, but amphetamine-class appetite suppression is still discussed in physique forums, and a 1966 journal paper compared Obetrol with diet therapy and phenmetrazine for weight loss.[1][3][4]
infobox: Not marketed; amphetamines are US Schedule II

paras: Obetrol was indicated for exogenous obesity as an aid to reducing appetite alongside a lower-calorie diet.[1][2] Grokipedia adds that doctors also used it off-label for attention problems in children before ADHD was formally defined; this comes from an AI-generated page.[2]

As a mixture of amphetamine and methamphetamine salts, Obetrol acted as a central nervous system stimulant, and appetite suppression was the effect for which it was prescribed.[1][2] Systematic reviews of amphetamine salts in ADHD report that they are among the best-supported ADHD medications but are associated with side effects such as hypertension and, in rare cases, psychotic symptoms.[5] A JACC review of stimulant ADHD therapies reported modest increases in resting heart rate and blood pressure, with case reports of arrhythmia and other cardiac events that were not shown to be causal.[6]

A 1966 report in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society compared weight losses under three regimens: diet therapy, phenmetrazine, and an amphetamine combination (Obetrol).[3] Beyond that, no modern trials of Obetrol itself were found. Later research on amphetamine salts concerns ADHD and stimulant-use disorders rather than weight loss.[5][6]

Rexar developed the product after wartime and postwar medical adoption of amphetamines, and marketed it during the era of widespread amphetamine diet-pill prescribing.[1][2] A 1970 FDA order required new applications for amphetamine products, and in September 1973 the agency withdrew Obetrol's approval, citing weak research evidence of efficacy.[1] Grokipedia also links the withdrawal to rising concern about amphetamine misuse during the period known as the speed epidemic.[2] Rexar moved production to Valley Stream, New York, and Richwood acquired it in 1993; the FDA issued a warning in 1994 before Adderall's ADHD approval in 1996.[1]

Grokipedia reports advertisements in the late 1960s and early 1970s promising rapid weight loss, and describes the drug as part of the broader amphetamine diet-pill era.[2] Obetrol now appears mostly as a historical forerunner of Adderall.

On T Nation, users who ask about appetite suppressants for lean-out phases mention a range of stimulants, and others in the community point out that mixed amphetamine salts are a different drug from methamphetamine.[4][7]
